input.workflow_summary: The developer wants an agent that continuously watches Twitter/X for public mentions of their brand (handle, keywords, hashtags), understands each mention and its conversational context, decides whether a response is warranted, and then automatically publishes a reply from the brand's X account — with tracking of what was posted and how it performed. The workflow therefore decomposes into: (0) mention discovery/streaming, (1) context enrichment, (2) content analysis/triage, (3) reply publication, (4) outcome tracking and audit. A critical constraint discovered during research is that X's own Automation Rules forbid keyword-search-triggered automated replies and require prior written approval from X for AI-powered reply bots, so the "automatically posts replies" half of the workflow must be designed around opt-in signals and human approval, not free-running keyword automation.
input.cross_task_notes:
Auth topology: the official path needs TWO credential types — an app-only OAuth 2.0 Bearer token for reads (search, lookup) and a user-context credential (OAuth 1.0a user context or OAuth 2.0 PKCE user token) for writes, because POST /2/tweets cannot be called app-only (docs.tweepy.org/en/stable/client.html). Ayrshare adds a third layer: its own API key + Profile-Key, plus, after 2026-03-31, your own X consumer key/secret passed as X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Key / X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Secret headers — so Ayrshare does not remove the need for an X developer app, it only removes OAuth plumbing and adds multi-network reach.

Cost topology: reads dominate volume. Official X API is credit-based pay-per-usage with 24h deduplication (docs.x.com/x-api/getting-started/about-x-api); TwitterAPI.io is ~$0.15/1K tweets with a $0.00015 per-call floor (twitterapi.io/pricing). A hybrid is economically attractive (cheap third-party reads + official writes) but note TwitterAPI.io is explicitly unaffiliated with X Corp, so a hybrid puts your read path outside X's Developer Agreement; that is a business/legal decision, not a technical one.

Tools that compose across tasks: search_brand_mentions (task 0) → get_mention_context (task 1) → score_mention (task 2) → draft_reply (LLM, not an external API) → human approval gate → post_reply (task 3) → record + get_reply_metrics (task 4). Reply-text generation itself is an LLM job, not an external API in this research; the MCP server should expose the analysis and publishing primitives and let the agent's model write the copy.

The single most important cross-cutting fact: help.x.com/en/rules-and-policies/x-automation states plainly that "sending automated replies to posts based on keyword searches alone is not permitted" and that AI reply bots need prior written approval from X. Any MCP server built for this workflow should encode that as a hard architectural constraint — the publish tool must require an explicit, auditable trigger reason (opt-in mention/reply/DM) plus a per-user one-reply cap plus an opt-out list, and ideally a human-in-the-loop approval step. Building it as a fully autonomous keyword-to-reply loop risks account suspension, which is a far larger cost than any API fee.

tasks.task_description: Monitor/search Twitter/X for mentions of a brand (handle, keywords, hashtags) in near real-time.

recommended_apis.rationale: The only first-party, ToS-sanctioned source of X data, and the only source whose data you may lawfully act on inside X's Developer Agreement. It covers both branches of mention monitoring: the account's own mentions timeline (high-precision, and importantly the signal X itself treats as opt-in intent) and general keyword search for unhandled brand mentions. Because the reply half of this workflow must run on official credentials anyway, using the official API for reads keeps the whole pipeline under one agreement.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /2/users/:id/mentions — mentions timeline for the brand account (the compliance-safe trigger source). GET /2/tweets/search/recent — keyword/hashtag search over the last ~7 days for brand terms. GET /2/tweets/search/all — full-archive search (elevated access). X docs also advertise real-time streaming of posts, which is the intended mechanism for continuous monitoring rather than polling search.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Pricing is credit-based pay-per-usage; monitoring a busy brand term can generate a large read volume, though X applies 24-hour deduplication so re-fetching the same resource within a day is charged once. Access tiers/entitlements for full-archive search and streaming are not documented on the pages that were reachable. The official docs site (docs.x.com) was largely blocked to automated fetching during this research, so endpoint-level parameters (max_results, since_id, tweet.fields, stream rule syntax) were verified via the Tweepy endpoint mapping rather than the primary source.
open_questions: What is the exact credit cost per read for search/recent and per stream-delivered post at current pricing?
Is the filtered-stream (rule-based real-time) endpoint available on standard pay-per-usage access, or does it require an elevated/enterprise entitlement?
What are the current rate limits on GET /2/users/:id/mentions and GET /2/tweets/search/recent?
Does full-archive search (/2/tweets/search/all) still require a separate approval or higher tier?

recommended_apis.rationale: A dramatically cheaper read layer with monitoring primitives that map almost one-to-one onto this workflow: webhook/websocket tweet filter rules, a per-user real-time tweet monitor, and a dedicated mentions endpoint. Auth is a single API key header, so prototyping is fast. It is a credible choice for the *listening* half only — it is explicitly not affiliated with X Corp, so it should not be treated as an official channel.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /twitter/tweet/advanced_search — full Twitter advanced-search operator syntax (OR, from:, since_time:, until_time:), queryType=Latest|Top, cursor pagination, ~20 tweets/page. GET /twitter/user/mentions — mentions by screen name, 20/page, newest first. Webhook/Websocket filter rule CRUD (add/get/update/delete rule) plus add/remove user-to-monitor endpoints for push-based real-time delivery.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Unofficial third-party provider that resells scraped X data; using it places your read path outside X's Developer Agreement and exposes you to breakage if X changes internals. Pricing is per returned item ($0.15/1K tweets, $0.18/1K profiles) with a $0.00015 per-call floor, so high-frequency polling of a quiet keyword still costs money. Rules must be explicitly activated after creation (default rule is not activated). No SLA guarantees were verified.
open_questions: What is the actual latency of webhook/websocket delivery versus X's own streaming?
Are filter rules billed per delivered tweet at the same $0.15/1K rate?
Does using this provider's data to drive posts on your own X account create a Developer Agreement issue for the account? (legal review needed)

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: Expose two distinct read tools rather than one generic 'search' tool, because they carry different compliance weight: (1) list_brand_mentions(since_id, max_results) backed by GET /2/users/:id/mentions — this is the opt-in-intent stream and should be the default trigger source for any reply flow; (2) search_brand_keywords(query, since_time, limit) backed by GET /2/tweets/search/recent (or TwitterAPI.io advanced_search in a cost-optimised deployment) — explicitly documented in its tool description as a LISTENING/ANALYTICS tool whose results must not be used to auto-trigger replies. Add register_stream_rule / list_stream_rules as separate tools if you use push delivery, but do NOT expose delete_stream_rule to the agent unattended (silently deleting a rule blinds the whole pipeline). Every returned mention should be normalised to a common shape (id, conversation_id, author, text, created_at, in_reply_to_id, is_reply, metrics) so the downstream tools are source-agnostic and you can swap the official API for a cheaper provider without touching agent prompts. Include a cursor/since_id state parameter so the agent cannot accidentally re-scan and re-trigger on already-processed mentions.

tasks.task_description: Retrieve context for a matched mention (author profile, parent tweets, full conversation thread) to inform a reply.

recommended_apis.rationale: Provides all the context primitives needed — the parent post, the author profile, the author's recent posts, and conversation reconstruction via conversation_id, which X documents as a first-class feature for tracking replies across a full thread. Using the same API as the trigger and the write keeps identity and entitlements consistent.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /2/tweets/:id and GET /2/tweets (batch lookup) with expansions to pull the referenced/parent post and author in one call. GET /2/users/by/username/:username and GET /2/users/:id for author profile. GET /2/users/:id/tweets for the author's recent history. GET /2/tweets/:id/quote_tweets for quote context. Thread reconstruction is done by querying recent search with conversation_id:<id>.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Thread reconstruction is not a single endpoint — you must combine conversation_id with search, which means a thread older than the recent-search window may be unreconstructable without full-archive access. Each expansion/lookup is a billable read. Field/expansion syntax is verbose and easy to get wrong; the primary docs pages describing fields and expansions could not be fetched during this research.
open_questions: Is conversation_id search still limited to the 7-day recent-search window on standard access?
What is the maximum number of ids per batch GET /2/tweets call under current pricing/limits?
Does requesting expansions increase credit consumption per request?

recommended_apis.rationale: Offers a purpose-built thread_context endpoint that returns the whole reply chain (ancestors and descendants) from a single tweet id — functionality that on the official API requires stitching conversation_id search together yourself. The tweet objects also embed a rich author profile (follower count, verification, account age, isAutomated flag), which is exactly the signal set you want for deciding whether a mention deserves a reply, and it comes without an extra profile lookup.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /twitter/tweet/thread_context?tweetId=&cursor= — returns t1..tN of the surrounding thread. GET /twitter/tweet/replies (and replies_v2 with Relevance/Latest/Likes sorting). GET /twitter/user/info by screen name, plus batch user lookup by ids. Every tweet object embeds an author UserInfo with followers, isBlueVerified, isAutomated, createdAt, description.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Documented pagination caveats: page size is not settable and has_next_page can return true even when no further data exists — your pagination loop must tolerate empty pages or it will spin. Unofficial provider (same ToS caveat as task 0). Cost is per returned tweet, so deep threads are proportionally expensive.
open_questions: How deep into a long thread does thread_context reliably reach before pagination degrades?
Is the embedded author object charged as a profile read on top of the tweet read?

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: Expose ONE composite tool, get_mention_context(tweet_id, include_thread=bool, include_author_history=bool), rather than mirroring the four or five underlying endpoints. Agents given raw lookup/expansion tools tend to make many redundant billable calls; a single composite tool lets you fan out server-side, cache aggressively (mention context is immutable enough to cache for hours, and the official API's 24h dedup means re-fetching is cheap but not free), and return one compact JSON blob shaped for prompt insertion. Bound it: cap thread depth and author-history length with server-side limits so the agent cannot request a 500-post thread. Deliberately do NOT expose follower/following list enumeration or bulk follower-ID pulls through this server — they are expensive, they are not needed to write a reply, and they turn a support-reply tool into an audience-scraping tool.

tasks.task_description: Analyze mention content (sentiment, intent, spam/toxicity) to decide whether and how to reply.

recommended_apis.rationale: The best fit for the specific decision this workflow must make, which is not really 'is this positive or negative' but 'is it safe and appropriate for my brand account to auto-reply to this'. X's automation rules explicitly recommend filtering responses based on potentially sensitive language in handles, display names and post text; Perspective's TOXICITY-family attributes are purpose-built for exactly that gate, return calibrated 0-1 probabilities, and support a scoreThreshold so you only get back scores above your cut-off.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST https://commentanalyzer.googleapis.com/v1alpha1/comments:analyze with {comment:{text}, requestedAttributes:{TOXICITY:{}, ...}, languages:[...], doNotStore:bool} → attributeScores[name].summaryScore.value (PROBABILITY, 0-1) plus optional per-sentence spanScores. POST .../comments:suggestscore exists for feedback but is not needed here.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: The endpoint is still on a v1alpha1 path. Crucially, doNotStore defaults to FALSE, meaning submitted text may be retained by Google for research/model improvement unless you explicitly set it true — for brand-monitoring content this should be reviewed and probably set to true by default. Attribute availability varies by language, and the docs note there is no simple way to use the API uniformly across production-supported and experimental languages. Access provisioning (quota request process) was not verified.
open_questions: What is the current quota-request/approval process and free-tier QPS for Perspective API?
Which attributes beyond TOXICITY (SEVERE_TOXICITY, INSULT, THREAT, SPAM) are production-supported for your target languages?
Should doNotStore be set true for third-party user content under your privacy policy?

recommended_apis.rationale: The right tool for the complementary question — the emotional valence of the mention, used to route (angry customer → escalate to human; praise → light acknowledgement; neutral question → templated answer). It returns both a signed score and a magnitude, plus per-sentence breakdown, which is more actionable than a single label for deciding escalation. It is a mature, stable GA API rather than an alpha path.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST https://language.googleapis.com/v2/documents:analyzeSentiment with {document:{type:'PLAIN_TEXT', content}, encodingType:'UTF8'} → documentSentiment.score (-1..1) and .magnitude, plus per-sentence sentiment and detected language. Language is auto-detected when language_code is omitted.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Auth is heavier than an API key: the documented example uses a Google Cloud service account / Application Default Credentials bearer token, which means GCP project setup, billing enablement and credential rotation. One document per request (no batching in the documented call), so per-mention cost and latency scale linearly. Sentiment on short, sarcastic, emoji-heavy social text is a known weak spot for generic sentiment models. Pricing was not fetched during this research.
open_questions: Current per-1000-units pricing and free tier for analyzeSentiment?
Does short-form social text accuracy justify a dedicated API over asking the agent's own LLM to classify?
Is there a batch endpoint to reduce per-mention overhead?

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: Expose a single score_mention(text, author_meta) tool that fans out to BOTH providers server-side and returns a fused, decision-shaped verdict: {sentiment_score, toxicity_score, is_question, recommended_action: 'auto_reply' | 'human_review' | 'ignore', reasons[]}. Returning raw provider payloads to the agent invites it to rationalise around thresholds; returning a policy verdict keeps the safety gate deterministic and in your code, not in the prompt. Hard-code the abstention rules on the server: any toxicity above threshold, any strongly negative sentiment, any mention from an account flagged isAutomated, or any mention already replied to → recommended_action must be 'human_review' or 'ignore', never 'auto_reply'. Always send doNotStore=true to Perspective. Note that reply *drafting* is an LLM job for the calling agent, not a tool here — the MCP server should provide the evidence and the gate, not the prose.

tasks.task_description: Post a reply tweet to the matched mention, handling auth, rate limits, duplicate prevention and automation-policy compliance.

recommended_apis.rationale: The only sanctioned way to publish. X's own automation rules state that non-API automation such as scripting the X website 'may result in the permanent suspension of your account', which rules out browser-driving and credential-replay approaches for a brand account you cannot afford to lose. POST /2/tweets with a reply reference is the canonical path, and it uses proper OAuth user-context delegation rather than password sharing.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST /2/tweets — create a post; used with a reply reference to the target post id to publish a reply (X documents publishing 'posts, replies, and threads'). DELETE /2/tweets/:id — retract a bad automated reply. Writes require user-context auth (OAuth 1.0a user context or OAuth 2.0 PKCE user token); an app-only bearer token is not sufficient.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: The dominant challenge is policy, not code. Automated replies triggered by keyword search alone are prohibited; AI-generated reply bots require prior written and explicit approval from X, and brands running auto-response campaigns must request approval. Compliant operation additionally requires: one automated reply per user interaction, an easy opt-out that you honour promptly, and replying only to the user's original post. Technically, POST /2/tweets rate limits and the exact reply parameter name/shape could not be confirmed because docs.x.com blocked automated fetching; verify against the live manage-posts reference before implementing. Duplicate/near-duplicate replies across accounts are separately called out as spam.
open_questions: Exact request body shape for a reply (reply.in_reply_to_tweet_id) — confirm against the live POST /2/tweets reference.
What are the current POST /2/tweets rate limits per user and per app under pay-per-usage access?
What is the concrete process and turnaround for obtaining X's written approval for an AI reply bot?
Does an inbound @mention alone satisfy the opt-in test for your use case, or does X expect a stronger signal?

recommended_apis.rationale: A reasonable managed abstraction if the brand also replies on other networks, since one call replies across X, LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, Bluesky, TikTok and YouTube, and it can reply to comments that were made outside Ayrshare via the social comment id. It also gives you a built-in post/comment record for auditing. It does not, however, remove any X policy obligation, and after 2026-03-31 it no longer removes the need for your own X developer app.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST https://api.ayrshare.com/api/comments/reply/:commentId with {platforms:['twitter'], comment:'...'} → returns twitter.commentId, sourceCommentId and postUrl. GET /api/comments/:id to retrieve comments (including, per their changelog, the id of the tweet a comment replied to). Auth: Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY> plus Profile-Key for a specific sub-profile.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Cost floor is real: comment reply is gated to Premium ($149/mo) and above, with Launch at $299/mo and Business from $599/mo. From March 31 2026 every X operation additionally requires your own X consumer key/secret sent as X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Key and X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Secret headers, so you carry both an Ayrshare bill and an X developer app. It is an extra vendor in the critical write path, and its reply model is comment-centric (Ayrshare comment id or social comment id) rather than arbitrary-tweet-centric, which needs mapping work from a search-discovered mention.
open_questions: Can you reply to an arbitrary discovered tweet that is not a comment on one of your posts, using only its tweet id?
Does Ayrshare enforce or surface X's automation-rule constraints, or is compliance entirely on you?
What X-side rate limits apply when many sub-profiles share one BYO consumer key?

recommended_apis.rationale: Documented and cheap, but recommended AGAINST for this workflow. Its write path requires POSTing your account email, username, password and 2FA secret key to a third party to obtain a login_cookie — that is credential sharing rather than OAuth delegation, it defeats 2FA, and it is functionally the non-API automation that X's rules warn can result in permanent account suspension. Listed here so the trade-off is explicit rather than discovered later.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST /twitter/user_login_v2 (email + username + password + 2FA secret → login_cookie, ~$0.005/call), then create_tweet_v2 (~$0.003/call) for create/reply, delete_tweet_v2, like_tweet_v2, retweet_tweet_v2, send_dm_v2, upload_media_v2 — all requiring the login_cookie.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Severe: full account credential and 2FA-secret exposure to a third party; no OAuth scoping or revocation story short of a password change; brand account suspension risk under X's automation and platform-manipulation rules. Also note X prohibits automated likes outright, so the like endpoint should never be wired up regardless of provider.
open_questions: None that would change the recommendation — the credential model alone disqualifies it for a brand account.

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: This is where MCP design matters most. Expose exactly one write tool, post_reply(in_reply_to_tweet_id, text, trigger_reason, approval_token), and make it refuse to act unless all of the following server-side checks pass: (a) trigger_reason is an enumerated opt-in signal (inbound @mention of the brand, a reply to a brand post, or an inbound DM) — never 'keyword_match'; (b) the target author is not on the opt-out list; (c) no prior automated reply exists for this author/interaction, enforcing X's one-reply-per-interaction rule via an idempotency key on (author_id, conversation_id); (d) the text is not a near-duplicate of recent replies, since duplicative posting is explicitly spam under the X Rules; (e) the target post still exists (X's own recommendation is to re-check before replying); (f) a human approval token is present, unless and until you hold X's written approval for an AI reply bot. Make it a dry_run-by-default tool that returns the exact payload it *would* send. Do NOT expose from any provider: like/unlike (automated likes are prohibited), follow/unfollow, hide_reply (automated hiding is prohibited), send_dm (separate and stricter opt-in regime), delete_tweet unattended (keep retraction as a human-invoked tool), or any credential-login endpoint. Rate-limit and daily-cap the tool in the server itself rather than trusting the agent to pace itself.

tasks.task_description: Track posted replies and engagement outcomes, and keep an audit log for automated-posting compliance.

recommended_apis.rationale: Gives first-party metrics for the replies you published, including private metrics that no third party can see. Since you must hold X credentials to post anyway, reading back metrics on your own posts adds no new auth surface. It is also the source of truth for whether a reply still exists (not deleted or withheld), which matters for an audit trail.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /2/tweets/:id and GET /2/tweets (batch) requesting public metrics (likes, reposts, replies) and, for your own posts, private metrics (impressions, clicks) via tweet.fields. GET /2/users/:id/tweets to enumerate the brand account's recent posts including its replies.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Metrics reads are billable like any other read, so polling every reply frequently is wasteful — batch lookups and back off over time as posts age. Private metrics are only available for your own posts. The exact tweet.fields names for non-public/organic metric groups could not be confirmed because the fields/metrics doc pages were unreachable during this research.
open_questions: Exact tweet.fields values for private/non-public and organic metrics, and whether they require user-context auth.
Is there a retention window after which impressions/clicks stop being returned for older posts?
How does the 24h deduplication interact with polling the same post's metrics repeatedly?

recommended_apis.rationale: If replies are published through Ayrshare, its analytics endpoint gives a normalised, cross-network view keyed by the Ayrshare post id, which is convenient when the brand replies on several platforms and wants one dashboard. It also returns lastUpdated/nextUpdate so you know the freshness of cached metrics rather than guessing.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST https://api.ayrshare.com/api/analytics/post with {id: <Ayrshare post id>, platforms:['twitter', ...]} → per-platform analytics object with engagement counts plus lastUpdated and nextUpdate timestamps.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Only covers posts made through Ayrshare, so it cannot report on replies you published directly via the X API — you must commit to one publishing path or reconcile two. Analytics depth is described as Basic on the $149 Premium tier and Advanced only from Launch ($299) upward. Metrics appear to be cached/refreshed on Ayrshare's schedule (nextUpdate) rather than real-time on demand.
open_questions: Which specific X/Twitter metric fields are returned, and are impressions included?
What is the refresh cadence implied by nextUpdate, and can it be forced?
Does 'Basic' analytics on Premium omit X metrics that the workflow needs?

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: Two tools plus one non-API responsibility. Expose get_reply_metrics(reply_ids[]) as a BATCH tool only — never a single-id tool, since agents will otherwise loop and burn credits one read at a time — returning a normalised {reply_id, likes, replies, reposts, impressions?, fetched_at} shape. Expose list_recent_automated_replies(since, limit) reading from your own datastore, not from the platform. The audit log itself should be local, written synchronously by the post_reply tool, and should capture the fields a compliance review would ask for: target tweet id, target author id, trigger_reason, the opt-in evidence, the scores from score_mention, the approval token/approver, the exact text posted, the resulting post id and URL, and any opt-out request received. Also expose add_to_optout(author_id) and is_opted_out(author_id) as first-class tools, because X requires you to honour opt-out requests promptly and that obligation needs to be machine-enforceable rather than a note in a runbook. Do not expose account-level or competitor analytics through this server; it widens scope well beyond replying and pulls in data you have no operational need to hold.

name: finalize_report
content: Report accepted.

state.goal: An agent that monitors Twitter/X for mentions of my brand and automatically posts replies.
tasks: Monitor/search Twitter/X for mentions of a brand (keywords, @handle, hashtags) in near real-time
Retrieve context for a matched mention (author profile, conversation thread, parent tweets) to inform a reply
Analyze mention content (sentiment, intent, spam/toxicity classification) to decide whether and how to reply
Post a reply tweet to the matched mention (and handle media/rate limits/duplicate prevention)
Track posted replies and engagement outcomes / audit log for automated posting compliance

findings.note: X API v2 officially supports searching, looking up and streaming posts in real time, publishing posts/replies/threads, conversation tracking via conversation_id, and engagement metrics. Base URL api.x.com/2. Access requires signing up at console.x.com, creating an app and getting credentials.
X API v2 uses pay-per-usage, credit-based pricing (no subscription); credits are deducted per request, and the same resource requested twice within 24 hours is only charged once (deduplication).

Third-party, unaffiliated-with-X data provider. Pay-per-use pricing: $0.15 per 1K tweets returned, $0.18 per 1K user profiles, followers from $0.01/1K; minimum $0.00015 (15 credits) per API call; credits never expire; no minimum spend. Explicitly states it is not affiliated with X Corp.

GET https://api.twitterapi.io/twitter/tweet/advanced_search takes a full Twitter advanced-search query string (operators like OR, from:, since_time:, until_time:), queryType=Latest|Top, cursor pagination; auth is a single X-API-Key header (no OAuth). Returns ~20 tweets/page with author object, conversationId, inReplyToId, entities and public metrics.

Offers real-time monitoring primitives: add/get/update/delete Webhook/Websocket tweet filter rules, plus add/remove users to monitor tweets in real time; also a dedicated 'Get User Mentions' endpoint (by screen name, 20 mentions/page, cursor, ordered by mention time desc).

Write actions (create/reply tweet v2, delete, like, retweet, DM, upload media) require a login_cookie obtained from /twitter/user_login_v2, which takes the account's email, username, PASSWORD and 2FA secret key — i.e. full account credential sharing, not OAuth. Trial prices: login $0.005/call, create tweet $0.003/call, like/retweet $0.002/call.

POST https://api.ayrshare.com/api/comments/reply/:commentId with Bearer API key + optional Profile-Key header posts a reply on X/Twitter (and Bluesky, FB, IG, LinkedIn, TikTok, YouTube). Can reply to a comment made outside Ayrshare using the Social Comment ID from GET /comments. Response returns twitter.commentId and postUrl. Feature available on Premium, Launch, Business, Enterprise plans only.

Starting March 31, 2026 all X operations through Ayrshare require bring-your-own X API credentials: after linking X via OAuth you must send X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Key and X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Secret headers (one X developer app reused across sub-profiles). Pricing starts at $149/mo (Premium, 1 social profile), $299/mo Launch (10 profiles, webhooks), $599/mo Business; 28-day free trial on Launch.

X Automation Rules (updated April 2026): "sending automated replies to posts based on keyword searches alone is not permitted." Automated replies/mentions are only allowed if the user opted in (e.g. replied to your post or DM'd you, or mentioned you in a way clearly inviting a response), you offer an easy opt-out, you send only ONE automated reply per user interaction, and the reply is to the user's original post. A user merely following you is NOT sufficient intent.

AI-powered automated reply bots are permitted ONLY with prior written and explicit approval from X (request via dedicated contact or developer portal). Advertisers/brands running auto-response campaigns must also request approval from X. Non-API automation (scripting the X website) may cause permanent account suspension. Automated likes and hide-replies are prohibited outright.

POST https://language.googleapis.com/v2/documents:analyzeSentiment with a Document {type: PLAIN_TEXT, content} returns documentSentiment.score (-1..1) and magnitude plus per-sentence sentiment; language auto-detected if language_code omitted. Auth is a Google OAuth2 bearer token / service-account ADC (not a simple API key in the documented example).

POST https://commentanalyzer.googleapis.com/v1alpha1/comments:analyze with {comment:{text}, requestedAttributes:{TOXICITY:{}, ...}} returns attributeScores[name].summaryScore.value probabilities 0-1, optional spanScores and scoreThreshold filtering; doNotStore flag controls whether submitted text is retained (defaults to false = data may be stored).

GET /twitter/tweet/thread_context?tweetId=&cursor= returns the full reply chain around a tweet (ancestors and descendants), with each Tweet carrying author UserInfo (followers, isBlueVerified, isAutomated, description, createdAt), conversationId, inReplyToId/Username and isLimitedReply. Pagination size is not controllable and has_next_page can be true even when no more data exists (documented Twitter-side inconsistency).

POST https://api.ayrshare.com/api/analytics/post with {id: <Ayrshare post id>, platforms:["twitter", ...]} returns per-platform post analytics (engagement counts, lastUpdated/nextUpdate timestamps); works for posts made through Ayrshare.

Relevant v2 read endpoints (per Tweepy's endpoint-to-method mapping table): GET /2/tweets/search/recent and GET /2/tweets/search/all for keyword search, and GET /2/users/:id/mentions for the authenticated brand account's mentions timeline. Client supports OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token (app-only) or OAuth 1.0a user context (consumer key/secret + access token/secret).

Context endpoints: GET /2/tweets/:id and GET /2/tweets (batch lookup), GET /2/users/:id, GET /2/users/by/username/:username, GET /2/users/:id/tweets, GET /2/tweets/:id/quote_tweets. Threads are reconstructed via conversation_id (X docs highlight conversation tracking) combined with recent search.

X API v2 exposes engagement metrics: public metrics (likes, reposts, replies) and private metrics (impressions, clicks) for your own posts, requested via tweet.fields; post lookup endpoints GET /2/tweets/:id and GET /2/tweets return them.

Replies are created with POST /2/tweets (Tweepy Client.create_tweet); deletion is DELETE /2/tweets/:id. Posting requires user-context auth (OAuth 1.0a user context or OAuth 2.0 PKCE user token), not app-only bearer.

report.workflow_summary: The developer wants an agent that continuously watches Twitter/X for public mentions of their brand (handle, keywords, hashtags), understands each mention and its conversational context, decides whether a response is warranted, and then automatically publishes a reply from the brand's X account — with tracking of what was posted and how it performed. The workflow therefore decomposes into: (0) mention discovery/streaming, (1) context enrichment, (2) content analysis/triage, (3) reply publication, (4) outcome tracking and audit. A critical constraint discovered during research is that X's own Automation Rules forbid keyword-search-triggered automated replies and require prior written approval from X for AI-powered reply bots, so the "automatically posts replies" half of the workflow must be designed around opt-in signals and human approval, not free-running keyword automation.

Because the reply half of this workflow must run on official credentials anyway, using the official API for reads keeps the whole pipeline under one agreement.

GET /2/tweets/search/recent — keyword/hashtag search over the last ~7 days for brand terms. GET /2/tweets/search/all — full-archive search (elevated access). X docs also advertise real-time streaming of posts, which is the intended mechanism for continuous monitoring rather than polling search.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Pricing is credit-based pay-per-usage; monitoring a busy brand term can generate a large read volume, though X applies 24-hour deduplication so re-fetching the same resource within a day is charged once. Access tiers/entitlements for full-archive search and streaming are not documented on the pages that were reachable. The official docs site (docs.x.com) was largely blocked to automated fetching during this research, so endpoint-level parameters (max_results, since_id, tweet.fields, stream rule syntax) were verified via the Tweepy endpoint mapping rather than the primary source.
open_questions: What is the exact credit cost per read for search/recent and per stream-delivered post at current pricing?
Is the filtered-stream (rule-based real-time) endpoint available on standard pay-per-usage access, or does it require an elevated/enterprise entitlement?
What are the current rate limits on GET /2/users/:id/mentions and GET /2/tweets/search/recent?
Does full-archive search (/2/tweets/search/all) still require a separate approval or higher tier?

recommended_apis.rationale: A dramatically cheaper read layer with monitoring primitives that map almost one-to-one onto this workflow: webhook/websocket tweet filter rules, a per-user real-time tweet monitor, and a dedicated mentions endpoint. Auth is a single API key header, so prototyping is fast. It is a credible choice for the *listening* half only — it is explicitly not affiliated with X Corp, so it should not be treated as an official channel.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /twitter/tweet/advanced_search — full Twitter advanced-search operator syntax (OR, from:, since_time:, until_time:), queryType=Latest|Top, cursor pagination, ~20 tweets/page. GET /twitter/user/mentions — mentions by screen name, 20/page, newest first. Webhook/Websocket filter rule CRUD (add/get/update/delete rule) plus add/remove user-to-monitor endpoints for push-based real-time delivery.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Unofficial third-party provider that resells scraped X data; using it places your read path outside X's Developer Agreement and exposes you to breakage if X changes internals. Pricing is per returned item ($0.15/1K tweets, $0.18/1K profiles) with a $0.00015 per-call floor, so high-frequency polling of a quiet keyword still costs money. Rules must be explicitly activated after creation (default rule is not activated). No SLA guarantees were verified.
open_questions: What is the actual latency of webhook/websocket delivery versus X's own streaming?
Are filter rules billed per delivered tweet at the same $0.15/1K rate?
Does using this provider's data to drive posts on your own X account create a Developer Agreement issue for the account? (legal review needed)

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: Expose two distinct read tools rather than one generic 'search' tool, because they carry different compliance weight: (1) list_brand_mentions(since_id, max_results) backed by GET /2/users/:id/mentions — this is the opt-in-intent stream and should be the default trigger source for any reply flow; (2) search_brand_keywords(query, since_time, limit) backed by GET /2/tweets/search/recent (or TwitterAPI.io advanced_search in a cost-optimised deployment) — explicitly documented in its tool description as a LISTENING/ANALYTICS tool whose results must not be used to auto-trigger replies. Add register_stream_rule / list_stream_rules as separate tools if you use push delivery, but do NOT expose delete_stream_rule to the agent unattended (silently deleting a rule blinds the whole pipeline). Every returned mention should be normalised to a common shape (id, conversation_id, author, text, created_at, in_reply_to_id, is_reply, metrics) so the downstream tools are source-agnostic and you can swap the official API for a cheaper provider without touching agent prompts. Include a cursor/since_id state parameter so the agent cannot accidentally re-scan and re-trigger on already-processed mentions.

tasks.task_description: Retrieve context for a matched mention (author profile, parent tweets, full conversation thread) to inform a reply.

recommended_apis.rationale: Provides all the context primitives needed — the parent post, the author profile, the author's recent posts, and conversation reconstruction via conversation_id, which X documents as a first-class feature for tracking replies across a full thread. Using the same API as the trigger and the write keeps identity and entitlements consistent.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /2/tweets/:id and GET /2/tweets (batch lookup) with expansions to pull the referenced/parent post and author in one call. GET /2/users/by/username/:username and GET /2/users/:id for author profile. GET /2/users/:id/tweets for the author's recent history. GET /2/tweets/:id/quote_tweets for quote context. Thread reconstruction is done by querying recent search with conversation_id:<id>.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Thread reconstruction is not a single endpoint — you must combine conversation_id with search, which means a thread older than the recent-search window may be unreconstructable without full-archive access. Each expansion/lookup is a billable read. Field/expansion syntax is verbose and easy to get wrong; the primary docs pages describing fields and expansions could not be fetched during this research.
open_questions: Is conversation_id search still limited to the 7-day recent-search window on standard access?
What is the maximum number of ids per batch GET /2/tweets call under current pricing/limits?
Does requesting expansions increase credit consumption per request?

recommended_apis.rationale: Offers a purpose-built thread_context endpoint that returns the whole reply chain (ancestors and descendants) from a single tweet id — functionality that on the official API requires stitching conversation_id search together yourself. The tweet objects also embed a rich author profile (follower count, verification, account age, isAutomated flag), which is exactly the signal set you want for deciding whether a mention deserves a reply, and it comes without an extra profile lookup.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /twitter/tweet/thread_context?tweetId=&cursor= — returns t1..tN of the surrounding thread. GET /twitter/tweet/replies (and replies_v2 with Relevance/Latest/Likes sorting). GET /twitter/user/info by screen name, plus batch user lookup by ids. Every tweet object embeds an author UserInfo with followers, isBlueVerified, isAutomated, createdAt, description.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Documented pagination caveats: page size is not settable and has_next_page can return true even when no further data exists — your pagination loop must tolerate empty pages or it will spin. Unofficial provider (same ToS caveat as task 0). Cost is per returned tweet, so deep threads are proportionally expensive.
open_questions: How deep into a long thread does thread_context reliably reach before pagination degrades?
Is the embedded author object charged as a profile read on top of the tweet read?

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: Expose ONE composite tool, get_mention_context(tweet_id, include_thread=bool, include_author_history=bool), rather than mirroring the four or five underlying endpoints. Agents given raw lookup/expansion tools tend to make many redundant billable calls; a single composite tool lets you fan out server-side, cache aggressively (mention context is immutable enough to cache for hours, and the official API's 24h dedup means re-fetching is cheap but not free), and return one compact JSON blob shaped for prompt insertion. Bound it: cap thread depth and author-history length with server-side limits so the agent cannot request a 500-post thread. Deliberately do NOT expose follower/following list enumeration or bulk follower-ID pulls through this server — they are expensive, they are not needed to write a reply, and they turn a support-reply tool into an audience-scraping tool.

tasks.task_description: Analyze mention content (sentiment, intent, spam/toxicity) to decide whether and how to reply.

recommended_apis.rationale: The best fit for the specific decision this workflow must make, which is not really 'is this positive or negative' but 'is it safe and appropriate for my brand account to auto-reply to this'. X's automation rules explicitly recommend filtering responses based on potentially sensitive language in handles, display names and post text; Perspective's TOXICITY-family attributes are purpose-built for exactly that gate, return calibrated 0-1 probabilities, and support a scoreThreshold so you only get back scores above your cut-off.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST https://commentanalyzer.googleapis.com/v1alpha1/comments:analyze with {comment:{text}, requestedAttributes:{TOXICITY:{}, ...}, languages:[...], doNotStore:bool} → attributeScores[name].summaryScore.value (PROBABILITY, 0-1) plus optional per-sentence spanScores. POST .../comments:suggestscore exists for feedback but is not needed here.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: The endpoint is still on a v1alpha1 path. Crucially, doNotStore defaults to FALSE, meaning submitted text may be retained by Google for research/model improvement unless you explicitly set it true — for brand-monitoring content this should be reviewed and probably set to true by default. Attribute availability varies by language, and the docs note there is no simple way to use the API uniformly across production-supported and experimental languages. Access provisioning (quota request process) was not verified.
open_questions: What is the current quota-request/approval process and free-tier QPS for Perspective API?
Which attributes beyond TOXICITY (SEVERE_TOXICITY, INSULT, THREAT, SPAM) are production-supported for your target languages?
Should doNotStore be set true for third-party user content under your privacy policy?

recommended_apis.rationale: The right tool for the complementary question — the emotional valence of the mention, used to route (angry customer → escalate to human; praise → light acknowledgement; neutral question → templated answer). It returns both a signed score and a magnitude, plus per-sentence breakdown, which is more actionable than a single label for deciding escalation. It is a mature, stable GA API rather than an alpha path.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST https://language.googleapis.com/v2/documents:analyzeSentiment with {document:{type:'PLAIN_TEXT', content}, encodingType:'UTF8'} → documentSentiment.score (-1..1) and .magnitude, plus per-sentence sentiment and detected language. Language is auto-detected when language_code is omitted.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Auth is heavier than an API key: the documented example uses a Google Cloud service account / Application Default Credentials bearer token, which means GCP project setup, billing enablement and credential rotation. One document per request (no batching in the documented call), so per-mention cost and latency scale linearly. Sentiment on short, sarcastic, emoji-heavy social text is a known weak spot for generic sentiment models. Pricing was not fetched during this research.
open_questions: Current per-1000-units pricing and free tier for analyzeSentiment?
Does short-form social text accuracy justify a dedicated API over asking the agent's own LLM to classify?
Is there a batch endpoint to reduce per-mention overhead?

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: Expose a single score_mention(text, author_meta) tool that fans out to BOTH providers server-side and returns a fused, decision-shaped verdict: {sentiment_score, toxicity_score, is_question, recommended_action: 'auto_reply' | 'human_review' | 'ignore', reasons[]}. Returning raw provider payloads to the agent invites it to rationalise around thresholds; returning a policy verdict keeps the safety gate deterministic and in your code, not in the prompt. Hard-code the abstention rules on the server: any toxicity above threshold, any strongly negative sentiment, any mention from an account flagged isAutomated, or any mention already replied to → recommended_action must be 'human_review' or 'ignore', never 'auto_reply'. Always send doNotStore=true to Perspective. Note that reply *drafting* is an LLM job for the calling agent, not a tool here — the MCP server should provide the evidence and the gate, not the prose.

tasks.task_description: Post a reply tweet to the matched mention, handling auth, rate limits, duplicate prevention and automation-policy compliance.

recommended_apis.rationale: The only sanctioned way to publish. X's own automation rules state that non-API automation such as scripting the X website 'may result in the permanent suspension of your account', which rules out browser-driving and credential-replay approaches for a brand account you cannot afford to lose. POST /2/tweets with a reply reference is the canonical path, and it uses proper OAuth user-context delegation rather than password sharing.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST /2/tweets — create a post; used with a reply reference to the target post id to publish a reply (X documents publishing 'posts, replies, and threads'). DELETE /2/tweets/:id — retract a bad automated reply. Writes require user-context auth (OAuth 1.0a user context or OAuth 2.0 PKCE user token); an app-only bearer token is not sufficient.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: The dominant challenge is policy, not code. Automated replies triggered by keyword search alone are prohibited; AI-generated reply bots require prior written and explicit approval from X, and brands running auto-response campaigns must request approval. Compliant operation additionally requires: one automated reply per user interaction, an easy opt-out that you honour promptly, and replying only to the user's original post. Technically, POST /2/tweets rate limits and the exact reply parameter name/shape could not be confirmed because docs.x.com blocked automated fetching; verify against the live manage-posts reference before implementing. Duplicate/near-duplicate replies across accounts are separately called out as spam.
open_questions: Exact request body shape for a reply (reply.in_reply_to_tweet_id) — confirm against the live POST /2/tweets reference.
What are the current POST /2/tweets rate limits per user and per app under pay-per-usage access?
What is the concrete process and turnaround for obtaining X's written approval for an AI reply bot?
Does an inbound @mention alone satisfy the opt-in test for your use case, or does X expect a stronger signal?

recommended_apis.rationale: A reasonable managed abstraction if the brand also replies on other networks, since one call replies across X, LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, Bluesky, TikTok and YouTube, and it can reply to comments that were made outside Ayrshare via the social comment id. It also gives you a built-in post/comment record for auditing. It does not, however, remove any X policy obligation, and after 2026-03-31 it no longer removes the need for your own X developer app.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST https://api.ayrshare.com/api/comments/reply/:commentId with {platforms:['twitter'], comment:'...'} → returns twitter.commentId, sourceCommentId and postUrl. GET /api/comments/:id to retrieve comments (including, per their changelog, the id of the tweet a comment replied to). Auth: Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY> plus Profile-Key for a specific sub-profile.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Cost floor is real: comment reply is gated to Premium ($149/mo) and above, with Launch at $299/mo and Business from $599/mo. From March 31 2026 every X operation additionally requires your own X consumer key/secret sent as X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Key and X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Secret headers, so you carry both an Ayrshare bill and an X developer app. It is an extra vendor in the critical write path, and its reply model is comment-centric (Ayrshare comment id or social comment id) rather than arbitrary-tweet-centric, which needs mapping work from a search-discovered mention.
open_questions: Can you reply to an arbitrary discovered tweet that is not a comment on one of your posts, using only its tweet id?
Does Ayrshare enforce or surface X's automation-rule constraints, or is compliance entirely on you?
What X-side rate limits apply when many sub-profiles share one BYO consumer key?

recommended_apis.rationale: Documented and cheap, but recommended AGAINST for this workflow. Its write path requires POSTing your account email, username, password and 2FA secret key to a third party to obtain a login_cookie — that is credential sharing rather than OAuth delegation, it defeats 2FA, and it is functionally the non-API automation that X's rules warn can result in permanent account suspension. Listed here so the trade-off is explicit rather than discovered later.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST /twitter/user_login_v2 (email + username + password + 2FA secret → login_cookie, ~$0.005/call), then create_tweet_v2 (~$0.003/call) for create/reply, delete_tweet_v2, like_tweet_v2, retweet_tweet_v2, send_dm_v2, upload_media_v2 — all requiring the login_cookie.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Severe: full account credential and 2FA-secret exposure to a third party; no OAuth scoping or revocation story short of a password change; brand account suspension risk under X's automation and platform-manipulation rules. Also note X prohibits automated likes outright, so the like endpoint should never be wired up regardless of provider.
open_questions: None that would change the recommendation — the credential model alone disqualifies it for a brand account.

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: This is where MCP design matters most. Expose exactly one write tool, post_reply(in_reply_to_tweet_id, text, trigger_reason, approval_token), and make it refuse to act unless all of the following server-side checks pass: (a) trigger_reason is an enumerated opt-in signal (inbound @mention of the brand, a reply to a brand post, or an inbound DM) — never 'keyword_match'; (b) the target author is not on the opt-out list; (c) no prior automated reply exists for this author/interaction, enforcing X's one-reply-per-interaction rule via an idempotency key on (author_id, conversation_id); (d) the text is not a near-duplicate of recent replies, since duplicative posting is explicitly spam under the X Rules; (e) the target post still exists (X's own recommendation is to re-check before replying); (f) a human approval token is present, unless and until you hold X's written approval for an AI reply bot. Make it a dry_run-by-default tool that returns the exact payload it *would* send. Do NOT expose from any provider: like/unlike (automated likes are prohibited), follow/unfollow, hide_reply (automated hiding is prohibited), send_dm (separate and stricter opt-in regime), delete_tweet unattended (keep retraction as a human-invoked tool), or any credential-login endpoint. Rate-limit and daily-cap the tool in the server itself rather than trusting the agent to pace itself.

tasks.task_description: Track posted replies and engagement outcomes, and keep an audit log for automated-posting compliance.

recommended_apis.rationale: Gives first-party metrics for the replies you published, including private metrics that no third party can see. Since you must hold X credentials to post anyway, reading back metrics on your own posts adds no new auth surface. It is also the source of truth for whether a reply still exists (not deleted or withheld), which matters for an audit trail.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: GET /2/tweets/:id and GET /2/tweets (batch) requesting public metrics (likes, reposts, replies) and, for your own posts, private metrics (impressions, clicks) via tweet.fields. GET /2/users/:id/tweets to enumerate the brand account's recent posts including its replies.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Metrics reads are billable like any other read, so polling every reply frequently is wasteful — batch lookups and back off over time as posts age. Private metrics are only available for your own posts. The exact tweet.fields names for non-public/organic metric groups could not be confirmed because the fields/metrics doc pages were unreachable during this research.
open_questions: Exact tweet.fields values for private/non-public and organic metrics, and whether they require user-context auth.
Is there a retention window after which impressions/clicks stop being returned for older posts?
How does the 24h deduplication interact with polling the same post's metrics repeatedly?

recommended_apis.rationale: If replies are published through Ayrshare, its analytics endpoint gives a normalised, cross-network view keyed by the Ayrshare post id, which is convenient when the brand replies on several platforms and wants one dashboard. It also returns lastUpdated/nextUpdate so you know the freshness of cached metrics rather than guessing.
recommended_apis.important_endpoints: POST https://api.ayrshare.com/api/analytics/post with {id: <Ayrshare post id>, platforms:['twitter', ...]} → per-platform analytics object with engagement counts plus lastUpdated and nextUpdate timestamps.
recommended_apis.potential_challenges: Only covers posts made through Ayrshare, so it cannot report on replies you published directly via the X API — you must commit to one publishing path or reconcile two. Analytics depth is described as Basic on the $149 Premium tier and Advanced only from Launch ($299) upward. Metrics appear to be cached/refreshed on Ayrshare's schedule (nextUpdate) rather than real-time on demand.
open_questions: Which specific X/Twitter metric fields are returned, and are impressions included?
What is the refresh cadence implied by nextUpdate, and can it be forced?
Does 'Basic' analytics on Premium omit X metrics that the workflow needs?

tasks.mcp_design_recommendation: Two tools plus one non-API responsibility. Expose get_reply_metrics(reply_ids[]) as a BATCH tool only — never a single-id tool, since agents will otherwise loop and burn credits one read at a time — returning a normalised {reply_id, likes, replies, reposts, impressions?, fetched_at} shape. Expose list_recent_automated_replies(since, limit) reading from your own datastore, not from the platform. The audit log itself should be local, written synchronously by the post_reply tool, and should capture the fields a compliance review would ask for: target tweet id, target author id, trigger_reason, the opt-in evidence, the scores from score_mention, the approval token/approver, the exact text posted, the resulting post id and URL, and any opt-out request received. Also expose add_to_optout(author_id) and is_opted_out(author_id) as first-class tools, because X requires you to honour opt-out requests promptly and that obligation needs to be machine-enforceable rather than a note in a runbook. Do not expose account-level or competitor analytics through this server; it widens scope well beyond replying and pulls in data you have no operational need to hold.

report.cross_task_notes:
Auth topology: the official path needs TWO credential types — an app-only OAuth 2.0 Bearer token for reads (search, lookup) and a user-context credential (OAuth 1.0a user context or OAuth 2.0 PKCE user token) for writes, because POST /2/tweets cannot be called app-only (docs.tweepy.org/en/stable/client.html). Ayrshare adds a third layer: its own API key + Profile-Key, plus, after 2026-03-31, your own X consumer key/secret passed as X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Key / X-Twitter-OAuth1-Api-Secret headers — so Ayrshare does not remove the need for an X developer app, it only removes OAuth plumbing and adds multi-network reach.

Cost topology: reads dominate volume. Official X API is credit-based pay-per-usage with 24h deduplication (docs.x.com/x-api/getting-started/about-x-api); TwitterAPI.io is ~$0.15/1K tweets with a $0.00015 per-call floor (twitterapi.io/pricing). A hybrid is economically attractive (cheap third-party reads + official writes) but note TwitterAPI.io is explicitly unaffiliated with X Corp, so a hybrid puts your read path outside X's Developer Agreement; that is a business/legal decision, not a technical one.

Tools that compose across tasks: search_brand_mentions (task 0) → get_mention_context (task 1) → score_mention (task 2) → draft_reply (LLM, not an external API) → human approval gate → post_reply (task 3) → record + get_reply_metrics (task 4). Reply-text generation itself is an LLM job, not an external API in this research; the MCP server should expose the analysis and publishing primitives and let the agent's model write the copy.

The single most important cross-cutting fact: help.x.com/en/rules-and-policies/x-automation states plainly that "sending automated replies to posts based on keyword searches alone is not permitted" and that AI reply bots need prior written approval from X. Any MCP server built for this workflow should encode that as a hard architectural constraint — the publish tool must require an explicit, auditable trigger reason (opt-in mention/reply/DM) plus a per-user one-reply cap plus an opt-out list, and ideally a human-in-the-loop approval step. Building it as a fully autonomous keyword-to-reply loop risks account suspension, which is a far larger cost than any API fee.
